To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the free energy of activation of an enzymatic reaction is a linear function of the free energy of the reaction in the absence of enzyme.

the analysis of free energy relationships using computational models can provide insight into the mechanisms of enzyme-catalysed group transfer reactions and can provide a quantitative basis for rational enzyme design.

The use of a common reference reaction in free energy relationships is a useful means of quantifying the influence of molecular changes on the extent of progress of reaction along a reaction coordinate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel synthetic methodology and mechanistic studies of organic reactions.
the development of new methods for the synthesis of biologically important molecules, particularly those of a heterocyclic nature.
understanding the mechanisms of enzyme-catalyed chemical transformations and the factors controlling the efficiency and specificity of these processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of linear free energy relationships in enzyme-catalyized reactions is not justified and that the use of nonlinear free energy relationships is not justified.

free energy relationships provide a powerful means of quantifying trends in reactivity with changing molecular structure, but that the choice of reference reaction is critical and that the interpretation of non-linearities is often difficult.

, although free energy relationships are a powerful and versatile tool for the study of enzyme catalysis and the prediction of enzyme-catalyze reaction rates, their application is not without its limitations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we are now at a point where we can make reliable predictions about how the reactivity of an enzyme will change when the structure of a substrate is altered, and that we can do so with a good understanding of the underlying physical principles.
the analysis of enzyme-catalyze group-transfer reactions using free energy relationships is best carried out using the most appropriate kinetic models and reference reactions.

the use of experimental free energy relationships in enzyme-catalyze reactions can provide a useful guide to the nature of the reaction coordinate and to the relative stabilities of the reactant, transition state and product.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of free energy relationships is a powerful tool for understanding the mechanisms of enzyme-catalysed reactions.
free energy relationships are a powerful and versatile means of characterizing and quantifying trends in rates of enzyme-catalyized reactions with changing molecular structure.
there are many ways to make a free energy relationship non-linear and that the choice of a reference reaction can be a critical determinant of the outcome.
